Breaking changes

New features
- Built-in support for soft deletes via the `paranoid` option.
- New `upsert()` method on all models.

- TypeScript definitions are now bundled; the separate types package is deprecated.
Bug fixes
- Fixed a memory leak when a transaction was rolled back after a timeout.
- Fixed incorrect escaping of JSON columns containing single quotes.
- Date columns no longer lose milliseconds when read from the database.

In this work we evaluate 14 RAG configurations on a corpus of 9,200 internal policy documents from three financial institutions, using 1,150 questions written and graded by domain experts. We find that retrieval quality, not model size, is the dominant factor: when the correct passage was among the top five retrieved chunks, answer accuracy was 87 percent on average, falling to 23 percent when it was not, regardless of which generator model was used. Chunking strategy had a larger effect than expected. Splitting documents by section headings rather than fixed token windows improved retrieval recall by 11 points, and adding a one-sentence document summary to each chunk added a further 6 points. Hybrid search combining keyword and embedding scores outperformed either alone, particularly for questions containing product codes or regulation numbers. Re-ranking retrieved passages with a cross-encoder improved accuracy by 4 points but tripled latency. Notably, 31 percent of wrong answers were stated with no hedging language, and expert graders judged these confident errors as the most harmful category. We also observed that accuracy on questions requiring information from two or more documents was only 41 percent in the best configuration. We conclude that organisations should invest in document preparation and retrieval evaluation before upgrading to larger models.

1. Introduction
Remote and hybrid work arrangements expanded rapidly after 2020, and a substantial body of research has since examined their effects on productivity, wellbeing and turnover. Most of this literature, however, treats remote work as a binary condition and relies on self-reported outcomes collected at a single point in time. Studies using objective performance data are rare and are concentrated in call-centre and software development settings, which limits generalisability to roles with high task interdependence. Moreover, the mechanisms through which hybrid schedules affect team-level outcomes remain under-theorised. Abstract
Background: Medication errors remain one of the leading causes of preventable harm in hospitals, and interruptions during medication rounds have been identified as a major contributing factor. Aim: This study aimed to evaluate the effect of a "do not disturb" tabard intervention on the frequency of interruptions and medication administration errors in adult medical wards. Methods: A quasi-experimental pre-post design with a non-equivalent control group was used. Data were collected through direct observation of 1,246 medication administrations by 58 nurses across four wards over sixteen weeks. Interruptions were classified by source and duration. Errors were identified by comparing observed administrations with prescription charts. Results: The mean number of interruptions per medication round decreased from 6.3 to 3.9 in the intervention wards (p<0.001), while no significant change was observed in the control wards. The administration error rate fell from 11.2% to 7.4%. Interruptions initiated by patients and relatives decreased most, whereas those initiated by other staff were largely unchanged. Nurses reported mixed attitudes toward the tabards, with some expressing concern about appearing unapproachable. Conclusion: Visual signalling may reduce interruptions, but should be combined with changes to team communication practices.

reading this for a management course (yes really). can you summarise the argument in a few sentences and tell me the main takeaway for someone who runs a team\n\nMax Weber regarded bureaucracy not as a pathology of modern life but as its most characteristic achievement. In his account, the bureaucratic office is defined by a clear hierarchy of authority, written rules that apply regardless of who occupies a position, appointment on the basis of technical qualification, and a strict separation between the official's private interests and the resources of the office. Compared with administration by notables, kinship or personal loyalty, such an organisation is faster, more predictable and less arbitrary; a citizen need not know anyone in order to be treated according to the rule. Yet Weber was deeply ambivalent about what this efficiency costs. The same impersonality that protects against favouritism also strips decisions of individual judgement and moral responsibility, since the official is trained to ask whether a procedure was followed rather than whether an outcome is good. As rational administration spreads from the state to the firm, the school and the hospital, people come to experience their working lives as movement within a structure they did not design and cannot easily question, a condition he famously described as an iron cage. Later critics have argued that Weber overstated the coherence of real bureaucracies, which are full of informal networks, discretion and rule-bending, and that these informal practices are often what allows the formal system to function at all.
